power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps ≥ .111", Text = "Attrition analyses revealed no significant differences in earlier MACH, S_WPC, or O_WPC scores between later participants and nonparticipants (all ps ≥ .111, |ds| ≤ .12; see Appendix Table A1)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: Machiavellianism is linked to workplace competition, yet it remains unclear whether this association reflects personality-driven activity effects, environment-driven reactivity effects, or a combination of both.
This study examined the reciprocal relationships between Machiavellianism and workplace competition across six years of early career development among 1,513 Belgian university graduates.

Using both Cross-Lagged Panel Models and Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models, we tested longitudinal activity and reactivity processes at the between-person and within-person levels, respectively.
To this end, workplace competition was evaluated using both objective occupational characteristics and subjective perceptions.

Regarding activity effects, results showed that higher levels of Machiavellianism at career start positively predicted increases in workplace competition (both objective and subjective), but only at the between-person level of analysis.

Additionally, results provided evidence for reactivity effects whereby higher workplace competition predicts increases in Machiavellianism, but only for subjective evaluations of competition and when analyzed at the between-person level.
Implications for theory and practice are discussed.
Originating in political philosophy, Machiavellianism describes a personality orientation shaped by beliefs about power, social systems, and interpersonal relations (Christie & Geis, 1970).
text.formatted: Originating in political philosophy, Machiavellianism describes a personality orientation shaped by beliefs about power, social systems, and interpersonal relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Christie & Geis, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, individuals high in Machiavellianism view social relationships as primarily competitive, which explains tendencies such as manipulativeness, cynicism toward others, and a strong focus on advancing one's own interests (Harms et al., 2024; Jones & Paulhus, 2014).
text.formatted: Specifically, individuals high in Machiavellianism view social relationships as primarily competitive, which explains tendencies such as manipulativeness, cynicism toward others, and a strong focus on advancing one's own interests <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Harms et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Jones & Paulhus, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In the work context, this orientation is associated with a range of detrimental outcomes, including workplace aggression (e.g., Linton & Power, 2013), bullying (e.g., Pilch & Turska, 2015), unethical conduct (e.g., Greenbaum et al., 2017) and more negative reactions to large-scale organizational change (e.g., Belschak et al., 2020).

text.text: Although the consequences of Machiavellianism have been well documented, understanding of the factors that shape Machiavellianism in organizational contexts remains limited.

Most research conceptualizes Machiavellianism as a stable antecedent variable that predicts workplace behaviors and outcomes, while paying relatively little attention to the external factors that may shape the development, activation, or expression of Machiavellian tendencies over time.

In contrast, contemporary personality research acknowledges that, alongside their relative stability, personality traits exhibit dynamic properties that allow them to adapt to environmental influences (Sosnowska et al., 2021; Tett et al., 2021; Wille et al., 2023), including features of the work environment (Woods et al., 2019).

text.text: Some research suggests that work-related situational cues can influence how Machiavellian tendencies are expressed in workplace behavior (e.g., Castille et al., 2017; De Hoogh et al., 2021).

text.text: Whether such work-related factors are also associated with changes in Machiavellianism over time remains unclear.

The early career stage following the transition from school to work represents a particularly formative period during which personality traits may adapt in response to new role demands and environmental pressures (McAdams & Olson, 2010; Woods et al., 2013; Woods et al., 2019).

text.text: With respect to Machiavellianism, the present study argues that workplace competition constitutes a particularly relevant environmental factor, given the trait's emphasis on strategic self-interest and manipulative tactics (Jones, 2025).

text.text: Specifically, workplace competition may function as a situational cue signaling that trait-relevant behaviors-such as prioritizing personal gain or exploiting others-are appropriate or rewarded (Tett & Burnett, 2003).

text.text: However, little is known about how Machiavellianism and workplace competition are dynamically related over time, particularly during the early career period, when both individual characteristics and environmental contexts are relatively malleable.

To address this gap, the present study examines the reciprocal relationships between Machiavellianism and workplace competition across the first six years of early career development following graduation, using repeated measurements at two-year intervals.

As an overarching theoretical framework, we draw on Person-Environment (P-E) fit theory (Kristof-Brown & Guay, 2011) which posits that the alignment between individual characteristics and environmental demands shapes work attitudes, behaviors, and outcomes (Van Vianen, 2018).

text.text: When individuals experience a high degree of fit, positive outcomes such as greater satisfaction and well-being are likely to emerge, whereas misfit is associated with psychological strain (Edwards, 1996; Krick et al., 2016).

text.text: Importantly, two complementary processes exist through which fit can be achieved or improved (Dawis & Lofquist, 1984; Edwards, 1996).
text.formatted: Importantly, two complementary processes exist through which fit can be achieved or improved <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dawis & Lofquist, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Edwards, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: First, activity refers to individuals' efforts to shape or select aspects of their work environment to better align with their needs and preferences.
Second, reactivity refers to individuals adapting their own characteristics to better meet environmental demands.

Building on this framework, the present study is the first to disentangle activity and reactivity processes linking Machiavellianism and workplace competition over the course of early career development.
In addition, the present study distinguishes between within-person and betweenperson effects to examine how activity and reactivity processes unfold over time (Hamaker et al., 2015).
text.formatted: In addition, the present study distinguishes between within-person and betweenperson effects to examine how activity and reactivity processes unfold over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hamaker et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In this longitudinal design, with assessments every two years over a six-year period, between-person effects capture longer-term, developmental processes, reflecting how stable interindividual differences in one variable (e.g., workplace competition) predict enduring changes in the other (e.g., Machiavellianism).

In contrast, within-person effects capture more dynamic processes, indicating how intraindividual changes in one variable, Machiavellianism and Workplace Competition relative to a person-specific baseline, predict subsequent changes in the other over time.

Therefore, disentangling within-person and between-person effects is essential for theory building, as it allows us to determine whether activity and reactivity processes operate through stable interindividual differences, dynamic intraindividual changes, or both (Hamaker, 2012).
text.formatted: Therefore, disentangling within-person and between-person effects is essential for theory building, as it allows us to determine whether activity and reactivity processes operate through stable interindividual differences, dynamic intraindividual changes, or both <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hamaker, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the present study conceptualizes workplace competition using both subjective perceptions and objective occupational characteristics, as each captures a distinct aspect of the interplay between individuals and work environments over time.

Subjective perceptions reflect individuals' experienced sense of competition (Fletcher et al., 2008), whereas objective characteristics capture structurally embedded competitive demands within occupations (Peterson et al., 2001).

text.text: This distinction is critical for clarifying the mechanisms underlying both activity and reactivity processes.

With respect to activity, objective indicators allow for the assessment of whether individuals high in Machiavellianism systematically select into occupations characterized by stronger competitive demands, reflecting preferences for particular types of environments.

Subjective indicators, in contrast, capture how such individuals perceive and construe their work environment, potentially reflecting heightened sensitivity to competitive cues or the attribution of competitive meaning without corresponding changes in objective conditions.

With respect to reactivity, objective competitive structures represent relatively stable environmental contingencies that, through sustained exposure, may contribute to enduring differences in personality development via reinforcement and internalization processes (Roberts et al., 2003).

text.text: Subjective perceptions, by contrast, function as more proximal situational cues that directly activate trait-relevant psychological states, thereby eliciting Machiavellian tendencies in response to perceived competitive demands (Tett & Burnett, 2003).

text.text: Taken together, the present study aims to make three key contributions to the literature on Machiavellianism in the work context.
First, it advances a more dynamic perspective on Machiavellianism by examining its developmental interplay with workplace characteristics.
Specifically, we focus on longitudinal interactions with workplace competition, given the conceptual relevance of this environmental demand for Machiavellian tendencies (e.g., Woods et al., 2019).

text.text: In doing so, the study is the first to investigate reciprocal relationships between Machiavellianism and workplace competition across a substantively meaningful time frame, namely the first six years of individuals' careers.
Second, to deepen understanding of these reciprocal relationships, we distinguish between between-person and within-person processes.
Both activity and reactivity mechanisms may operate at one or both levels, and disentangling these effects provides more precise insight into the longitudinal dynamics at play.
Importantly, the chosen time frame aligns with the theoretical mechanisms under investigation (Ployhart & Vandenberg, 2010).
text.formatted: Importantly, the chosen time frame aligns with the theoretical mechanisms under investigation <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Ployhart & Vandenberg, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Trait change at the between-person level is expected to unfold gradually and accumulate over extended periods, justifying the six-year longitudinal design.

At the same time, although within-person dynamics in personality can unfold across a range of temporal intervals, two-year lags were selected to capture meaningful changes in workplace competition and their potential implications for Machiavellianism.
Specifically, such intervals allow sufficient time for competitive norms to emerge, stabilize, or decline, and for individuals to perceive and internalize these dynamics.
Third, the present study distinguishes between objective and subjective indicators of workplace competition.

By integrating both operationalizations, the study clarifies the extent to which person-environment dynamics linking Machiavellianism and workplace competition are driven by perceptual, as opposed to structural, mechanisms (or vice versa).
Adopting a more dynamic and developmental perspective on Machiavellianism in relation to workplace competition also yields important practical implications.

Evidence for reactivity effects would challenge the assumption that Machiavellianism is fixed once individuals enter the labor market, instead suggesting that the trait remains malleable over the course of career development.

Moreover, the present study identifies a situational factorworkplace competition-that may either dynamically activate Machiavellian tendencies (i.e., at the within-person level) or contribute to more enduring changes in the trait (i.e., at the between-person level) over time.

text.text: The limited insight into the dynamic and developmental properties of Machiavellianism stands in contrast to seminal conceptualizations of the trait.

Early socialcognitive conceptualizations (e.g., Christie & Geis, 1970) portray Machiavellianism as rooted in a cynical belief that others are fundamentally self-interested, reflecting learned expectations and social schemas.

Similarly, within the Dark Triad framework, Machiavellianism is characterized by high environmental attunement-particularly compared to traits such as psychopathy-implying heightened sensitivity to situational cues and greater behavioral flexibility (Bereczkei et al., 2015; Bereczkei, 2018; Jones & Mueller, 2022).

text.text: Individuals high in Machiavellianism are thought to monitor environmental payoff structures and adjust their behavior accordingly.
When such strategies are consistently rewarded or penalized, trait-relevant patterns may become reinforced or attenuated over time.
Taken together, these theoretical perspectives point toward a more dynamic and developmentally sensitive view of Machiavellianism in the work context, which the present study seeks to advance.
Workplace competition represents a contextual feature with complex implications for employee functioning (Swab & Johnson, 2019).

text.text: Competitive work environments are characterized by negatively interdependent goals and relative performance evaluations, such that individuals' success often comes at the expense of others (Brown et al., 1998; Deutsch, 1949).

text.text: Although such environments can stimulate performance and innovation, they also foster conditions that encourage strategic and self-interested behavior, as individuals navigate inherently zero-sum dynamics (Fletcher et al., 2008).

text.text: Importantly, workplace competition can be conceptualized at both the objective and subjective level.

Objective competition reflects structural characteristics embedded in jobs, organizations or occupations, such as formal performance metrics, ranking systems, and reward structures that emphasize relative outcomes.
These features exist independently of employees' interpretations of their work environment (DeVaro, 2006).
text.formatted: These features exist independently of employees' interpretations of their work environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(DeVaro, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, subjective competition refers to employees' perceptions of interpersonal rivalry and the extent to which they feel compelled to outperform colleagues to succeed.

Psychological climate research conceptualized such perceptions as individually constructed interpretations of situational demands, rather than direct reflections of objective environmental conditions (James & James, 1989; Spurk et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Psychological climate research conceptualized such perceptions as individually constructed interpretations of situational demands, rather than direct reflections of objective environmental conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(James & James, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Spurk et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Both individuals' perceptions of workplace competition and their exposure to objectively competitive environments are closely intertwined with personality characteristics.

For example, individuals low in agreeableness or high in dominance and hostility are more likely to construe their work environment as competitive, even under comparable objective conditions (Brown et al., 1998; Fletcher et al., 2008; Ryckman et al., 1996).

text.text: Beyond such perceptual processes, personality traits are also systematically related to individuals' presence in objectively competitive environments.

Vocational development research shows that individuals lower in agreeableness are more likely to enter enterprising occupations characterized by selling, persuading, and relative performance demands, whereas more agreeable individuals tend to select people-oriented occupations emphasizing cooperation (Brown & Hirschi, 2013; Wille & De Fruyt, 2014).

text.text: Importantly, a major limitation of this body of research is its predominant reliance on cross-sectional designs, which preclude conclusions about the direction of effects.

text.text: In line with P-E fit principles, individuals high in Machiavellianism are motivated to seek and/or shape work environments that align with their strategic orientations.
Such activity processes may operate at both the between-person and within-person level.
At the between-person level, stable differences in Machiavellianism are expected to predict systematic differences in exposure to competitive work environments over time.
Specifically, individuals generally high in Machiavellianism are likely to select into and/or cultivate more competitive workplaces from initial career entry onward.

Competitive environments provide opportunities to deploy strategic and instrumental tactics with fewer constraints from cooperative norms, thereby enabling a stronger focus on individual goals and relative positioning (Brown et al., 1998).

Furthermore, Machiavellianism may exhibit within-person fluctuations over time, which are accompanied by corresponding changes in workplace competition.

Specifically, when Machiavellian tendencies temporarily intensify, individuals may perceive their current work context as less aligned with their dispositional orientation, thereby motivating efforts to increase the level of competition.

Such effects are consistent with P-E fit theory, which posits that fit perceptions are dynamic and responsive to changes in individuals' characteristics and experiences (Edwards & Shipp, 2007; Vleugels et al., 2018).

Reactivity processes describe how workplace competition may shape Machiavellianism over time.
In general, competitive work contexts can reinforce Machiavellian tendencies by repeatedly validating strategic, self-interested behavior as effective and appropriate.
Here again, it is useful to distinguish between processes operating at the within-person and between-person level.

At the between-person level, sustained exposure to workplace competition is expected to foster the longitudinal development of Machiavellianism by promoting the internalization of competitive orientations.
Specifically, repeated exposure to norms and practices that reward strategic, self-interested behavior may create a context conducive to the development of Machiavellian tendencies.

text.text: Building on this perspective and P-E fit theory, the present study examined reciprocal associations between Machiavellianism and workplace competition in a longitudinal panel of college alumni followed across their first six career years.
Results supported bidirectional effects, although these differed by level of analysis (within-vs. between-person) and by whether workplace competition was operationalized objectively or subjectively.

text.text: First, the results of this study provided clear evidence of activity effects whereby Machiavellianism positively predicted subsequent workplace competition at the betweenperson level.
Specifically, higher trait levels of Machiavellianism predicted gradual increases in competition over the course of the study.

These effects emerged for both objective and subjective measures of workplace competition, suggesting that individuals high in Machiavellianism progressively shape both their work environment and their perceptions thereof to become more competitive during the early stages of their careers.

The finding that Machiavellianism predicted both objective and subjective workplace competition suggests that the observed activity effect cannot be attributed solely to perceptual mechanisms, but rather operates through multiple pathways.
At the individual level, those high in Machiavellianism may actively seek out and shape roles and responsibilities that align with their strategic and self-interested goals (Swab & Johnson, 2019).
text.formatted: At the individual level, those high in Machiavellianism may actively seek out and shape roles and responsibilities that align with their strategic and self-interested goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Swab & Johnson, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, part of these activity effects can also be driven or strengthened by factors at the level of organizations, where Machiavellian characteristics such as strategic thinking may be valued and actively recruited because they align with structural demands for instance in competitive industries (Castille et al., 2017).
text.formatted: However, part of these activity effects can also be driven or strengthened by factors at the level of organizations, where Machiavellian characteristics such as strategic thinking may be valued and actively recruited because they align with structural demands for instance in competitive industries <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Castille et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, these dynamics are likely reinforced by differential retention processes: once embedded in competitive environments, individuals high in Machiavellianism may experience greater fit and thus be more likely to stay, whereas those lower in Machiavellianism may perceive misfit and be more likely to exit (Schneider, 1987).

text.text: Findings also indicated that activity effects emerged only at the between-person level and not at the within-person level.
Thus, no evidence was found for a dynamic adaptation process whereby intraindividual changes in Machiavellianism predict subsequent changes in workplace competition.

Instead, the influence of Machiavellianism on competition appears to reflect a gradual and cumulative process, in which stable individual differences-already present at career entry-shape subsequent selection into and/or modification of work environments.
The current study also provided evidence for reactivity effects, indicating that workplace competition can foster subsequent Machiavellianism.
Notably, this effect only emerged at the between-person level, such that stable differences in competition predicted gradual increases in Machiavellianism over time.

This finding suggests that competitive work environments may provide reward structures that encourage the expression of Machiavellian tendencies, which, through repeated trait activation (e.g., Wrzus & Roberts, 2017), eventually become reinforced and consolidated.

text.text: From this perspective, striving for P-E fit represents a key mechanism underlying reactivity, as individuals adapt their behavior, skills and attitudes to meet environmental demands and facilitate effective functioning (Dawis & Lofquist, 1984; Rossetti et al., 2025).

text.text: Importantly, the results further indicated that the between-person effect of workplace competition on subsequent Machiavellianism was limited to subjective perceptions of the competitive work climate, whereas no such reactivity effects emerged for objective indicators of workplace competition.

Previous research on how work affects personality development has produced mixed findings on the relative importance of objective and subjective work characteristics. Heyde et al. (2024), for instance, showed that only objective work activities focused on personal achievements fostered trait narcissism over time, whereas the diminishing effects of work activities centered around helping others were significant for both objective and subjective operationalizations.

text.text: Accumulating research findings will provide further insight into the status of objective and subjective characteristics depending on the specific trait that is being studied and the aspect of work (e.g., work conditions, work activities, work outcomes, etc.) that is considered.
Finally, no reactivity effects were observed at the within-person level.
Thus, intraindividual changes in workplace competition did not predict subsequent changes in Machiavellianism.

To our knowledge, this study is the first to examine reciprocal relationships between personality and work characteristics using the combination of CLPM and RI-CLPM approaches, whereas prior research has typically relied on approaches that confound between-person and within-person effects (Orth et al., 2021).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that the influence of workplace competition on Machiavellianism reflects a relatively stable developmental process, rather than a dynamic transactional process in which changes in the work environment translate into corresponding trait-level adaptations.

Over the past decade, applied personality research has broadened the conceptualization of traits to better account for a range of dynamic and developmental personality processes in work and career contexts (e.g., Wille & De Fruyt, 2014; Woods et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2026).

text.text: Yet, with few exceptions (e.g., Heyde et al., 2024; Spurk & Hirschi, 2018; Wille et al., 2019), this reconceptualization has been largely restricted to the so-called bright side of personality, such as the Big Five traits.

text.text: By showing that individual experiences of workplace competition contribute longitudinally to differences in Machiavellianism levels, the current study provides initial evidence that such reconceptualization of (dark side) Machiavellianism is also warranted.

The reconceptualization of Machiavellianism as a dynamic and developmental trait in work and career contexts represents an integration between early social-cognitive views of Machiavellianism (Christie & Geis, 1970) and contemporary process models of personality development (e.g., Woods et al., 2019; Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).

text.text: According to the socialcognitive view, Machiavellianism is construed on the basis of cynical beliefs about the intentions of others, which themselves are based on learned social schemas.
Importantly, these schemas are shaped by experience, which means that if workplace environments repeatedly confirm or disconfirm cynical expectations, then the belief system itself could shift.
It is here that process models of personality provide additional understanding of the mechanisms involved.

Specifically, repeated experience of environmental demands, processed through cognitive and affective reactions resulting in behavior, and observation of behavioral consequences, leads to typical, characteristic response patterns (Woods et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Specifically, repeated experience of environmental demands, processed through cognitive and affective reactions resulting in behavior, and observation of behavioral consequences, leads to typical, characteristic response patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Woods et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Through such processes, traits eventually become refined, strengthened or modified to better fit situational demands, providing a coherent theoretical foundation for the observed developmental (between-person) effect of workplace competition on Machiavellianism.

In addition to establishing such dynamic and developmental perspective on Machiavellianism, the present study also yielded first insights into some of the ways in which Machiavellianism and workplace competition reciprocally interact over time.
Specifically, an important factor that needs to be taken into account when theorizing reciprocal relationships between Machiavellianism and work concerns the level at which these effects unfold.

The current study suggests that the potential co-development of Machiavellianism and workplace competition resides primarily at the between-person level, whereby personal adaptation (in the case of reactivity effects) and environmental adjustment (in the case of activity effects) gradually accumulate over time, creating stable interindividual differences, rather than operating as highly dynamic and responsive intraindividual mechanisms.

Zooming in on reactivity, the distinction between within-person and between-person effects highlights a basic distinction between behavioral adjustment and trait change that can be integrated into theory of how Machiavellianism functions and unfolds in the work context.
Specifically, Machiavellianism combines a relatively stable cynical worldview about human nature with a flexible repertoire of instrumental tactics (Monaghan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Specifically, Machiavellianism combines a relatively stable cynical worldview about human nature with a flexible repertoire of instrumental tactics <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Monaghan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This structure means that momentary changes in competitive pressures can largely be absorbed at the tactical level without altering the core disposition.
For instance, when experienced competition increases, individuals may respond by deploying strategic tactics or becoming more selective in their cooperative interactions.
These tactical adaptations satisfy immediate environmental demands while leaving the underlying worldview and cynical belief system largely intact.
Trait change is likely only to emerge when such strategies consistently succeed or fail, and when the relevant disposition is repeatedly reinforced or challenged.
Interestingly, the reactivity effect of workplace competition on Machiavellianism was only significant for subjective perceptions of competition.

P-E fit perspectives emphasize that environmental influences are psychologically mediated, such that objective characteristics become developmentally consequential as far as they are perceived as salient and personally relevant (Edwards et al., 2006).
text.formatted: P-E fit perspectives emphasize that environmental influences are psychologically mediated, such that objective characteristics become developmentally consequential as far as they are perceived as salient and personally relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Edwards et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, work environments allow considerable room for construal, meaning that the same structural conditions may carry different meanings across individuals and over time (Deci & Ryan, 1987; Meyer et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Moreover, work environments allow considerable room for construal, meaning that the same structural conditions may carry different meanings across individuals and over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Deci & Ryan, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Meyer et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, subjectively experienced competition may more directly capture the functional input through which competitive contexts reinforce trait-congruent orientations.
In contrast, objective competition reflects more distal structural features whose developmental influence depends on whether they are perceived and engaged with.

In sum, our findings highlight that in theory on the impact of work on Machiavellianism, a distinction needs to be made between objective and subjective work characteristics, as both may capture distinct inputs into personality development.
The current findings regarding activity and reactivity effects carry potentially important practical implications for individuals as well as organizations.

From an individual perspective, our longitudinal study shows that Machiavellianism functions not only as an individual difference explaining work behavior (e.g., O'Boyle et al., 2012), but additionally as a career-shaping characteristic.
text.formatted: From an individual perspective, our longitudinal study shows that Machiavellianism functions not only as an individual difference explaining work behavior (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">O'Boyle et al., 2012)</ref>, but additionally as a career-shaping characteristic.

text.text: That is, individuals high in Machiavellianism gradually select into, evoke, or create increasingly competitive work environments, indicating that career experiences are partly constructed through personality-driven environmental change.
Consequently, seemingly small dispositional differences at career entry can accumulate into substantially different career experiences over time.
On the one hand, this process may be seen as positive from a P-E fit perspective, because individuals gravitate towards environments that align with their personality orientations.
However, on the other hand it is relevant for individuals and their career coaches to bear in mind that competition at work also comes with potential trade-offs.
Specifically, sustained exposure to workplace competition throughout one's career may increase the likelihood of adverse long-term health outcomes (Wittchen et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Specifically, sustained exposure to workplace competition throughout one's career may increase the likelihood of adverse long-term health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Wittchen et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the combination of activity and reactivity suggests that competitive environments can become self-reinforcing.
Specifically, workers high in Machiavellianism may enter a developmental pathway in which they increasingly encounter competitive conditions.
Such environments, in turn, may reward political skill, strategic behavior, and status striving, which could further strengthen competitive dynamics within teams and organizations.
In terms of interventions, organizations can reduce harmful outcomes by setting clear behavioral standards and enforcing them consistently (Pilch & Turska, 2015; Shah et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In terms of interventions, organizations can reduce harmful outcomes by setting clear behavioral standards and enforcing them consistently <ref type="bibr">(Pilch & Turska, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Shah et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This includes defining unacceptable behaviors, increasing transparency in key decisions, and applying predictable consequences when standards are violated.

Finally, the current findings suggest that when assessing workplace climate or evaluating conditions associated with Machiavellian behavior, incorporating measures of perceived competition may provide more accurate insights than relying solely on structural indicators of competition (Houston et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Finally, the current findings suggest that when assessing workplace climate or evaluating conditions associated with Machiavellian behavior, incorporating measures of perceived competition may provide more accurate insights than relying solely on structural indicators of competition <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Houston et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the present results indicate that employees' subjective experience of competition may be at least as important as objective competitive conditions in shaping personality-environment dynamics.

Consequently, interventions aimed at reducing dysfunctional competitive dynamics may need to address not only organizational structures, but also employees' perceptions and interpretations of those structures.
This study was conducted in a cohort of Belgian college alumni who were followed across the first six years of their professional careers.
Although this cohort design offers several advantages, such as ensuring that all participants face similar career challenges, it also comes with a number of limitations.
First, all participants were highly educated, which could have affected the likelihood of activity effects.
Specifically, one could argue that the careers of individuals with higher education offer greater flexibility to make choices and changes that accommodate personal preferences and strivings.
Future research using a more educationally diverse sample could investigate whether activity processes are equally present in the careers of individuals with different educational backgrounds.

Second, the present study focused on the initial career stage because (a) this period is often characterized by intense professional exploration, with starting professionals opening new doors in pursuit of P-E fit, and (b) personality traits are most malleable during this stage of adulthood (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Second, the present study focused on the initial career stage because (a) this period is often characterized by intense professional exploration, with starting professionals opening new doors in pursuit of P-E fit, and (b) personality traits are most malleable during this stage of adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Future research is needed to examine whether activity and reactivity effects unfold similarly across different career and life stages.
For instance, it could investigate the age at which Machiavellianism matures to the point where workplace factors no longer exert pervasive effects on the trait.
Relatedly, future research could adopt different timeframes to study reciprocal effects between Machiavellianism and work.
A limitation of the current two-year intervals is that short-term within-person dynamics, occurring across months, weeks, or even days, cannot be captured.
Personality dynamics research suggests that state-level variability differs substantially across traits and contexts (Nübold et al., 2022; Kuijpers et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Personality dynamics research suggests that state-level variability differs substantially across traits and contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Nübold et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Kuijpers et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of within-person effects in the current RI-CLPM analyses may indicate genuine trait stability, but it may also reflect that the measurement intervals were too long to capture shorter-term dynamics.

Future research using intensive longitudinal designs, such as experience sampling or daily diary methods, could establish whether Machiavellianism shows meaningful state-level fluctuations and, if so, the extent to which workplace competition triggers such variation.
Finally, future research could extend this dynamic and developmental perspective by examining other workplace characteristics and experiences.
At the individual level, experiences of job insecurity, for instance, may lead people to prioritize self-preservation and engage in covert tactics to remain relevant.
At the team or organizational level, toxic leadership may model Machiavellian behavior, which can spread through teams and create behavioral norms that employees internalize.
In contrast, a strong ethical work climate may establish clear moral boundaries for appropriate behavior, thereby buffering the development of Machiavellianism among employees.
A defining characteristic of Machiavellianism is its sensitivity to environmental opportunities and constraints, accompanied by strategic behavioral adjustment.
Therefore, understanding the role of this Dark Triad trait in work and career contexts requires a longitudinal perspective in which Machiavellianism both shapes and is shaped by the work environment.

The present study provided evidence that workplace competition is one such environmental factor: individuals higher in Machiavellianism tend to seek out more competitive work environments, while experiencing workplace competition also contributes to the longitudinal development of this trait.

Together, these findings underscore the dynamic interplay between personality and work environments and highlight the importance of adopting developmental and transactional perspectives in future research across different personality traits, workplace characteristics, career stages, and timescales.
